utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Tolimir, is the next witness ready to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not necessarily mine. The Defence believes that the witness is ready. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness should be brought in, please. I think we have a problem with the transcript in e-court. It stopped at the beginning of the words of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Usher should assist so that the witness can hear. Do you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I do. Now I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very good. Again, welcome to the courtroom. Good morning, and please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I state for the record that the transcript is now working in e-court. Sir, Mr. Tolimir is now putting questions to you during his examination-in-chief, followed by the Prosecutor. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Culic. May God-speed be with you and may God's will be done in today's hearing and not necessarily mine. I greet you on behalf of Defence. I would like to thank you for being here. Since we speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to look at the screen in front of you and you will see that our words are being transcribed. I would kindly ask you to start giving your answer only when the transcript has stopped. I'll do the same. After my every question I will say "thank you" which will be your clue to start answering.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Thank you, general, sir. And I wish you all the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My first question to you is this: Can you state your full name for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: My name is Slavko Culic. I was born on the 5th October, 1958, in Glavica, Glamoc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us something about your military education. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I completed the secondary military school of the land army. I specialised in infantry training. Thereafter I graduated from the military academy of the land army. Again, I specialised in infantry training. In the course of my service, I successfully completed training courses and became company commander, battalion commander. I passed a test to become major. And I also passed the entrance exam for the command staff continuous education. During the course of my service, I attended some other minor training courses in order to improve my skills with regard to the aforementioned specialties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you graduate from the secondary school? When did you graduate from the academy? And when did you complete the training courses for a company and battalion commanders, was that before the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the secondary military school in 1977 in Sarajevo. I graduated from the military academy in 1980. In 1983 I attended a training course for company commander, and I completed the training course for battalion commander in 1987 and 1988. Which means all the training courses I did happened before the war started in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Can you tell us something about your professional career before the year 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: When I graduated from the military academy in 1980, I was assigned to work in the military academy of the land army. I was the commander of an education group of cadets. From 1983, I was transferred to the Brijuni garrison. I was the commander of a navy infantry company there. From 1987 until 1990, I worked at the Mali Losinj garrison. I was a company commander there. From 1990 to 1991, I worked at the Pula garrison. I was the deputy commander and battalion commander. When the war broke out in the territory of the Republic of Croatia in 1991, I was transferred to the Niksic garrison where I served as battalion commander as well. I stayed at the Niksic garrison until May 1992; that is when I was transferred to the 5th Corps, to the Mrkonjic Grad garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, When did you become a member of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: It was on the 19th of May, 1992, when I reported to the Army of Republika Srpska at the Banja Luka garrison, and from then I have been a member of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your establishment post when you reported to the Army of Republika Srpska? And then what happened during the war; what establishment post did you occupy throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: When I reported to the Army of Republika Srpska at the Banja Luka garrison, to be more precise, I was appointed the commander of what was then the 1st Krajina Brigade at the Mrkonjic Grad garrison. I started working on the 10th of June, 1992, and I remained in that position until the end of the war and even after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. After the end of the war, what was your establishment post?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: After the end of the war in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was still the commander of an infantry brigade, and that brigade was the 113th Brigade at the Mrkonjic Grad garrison. And I remained at that position until the year 2003, and that's when I was pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. And now can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you knew Zdravko Tolimir and since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I know General Zdravko Tolimir personally. I met him in 1992 and I knew of him even before, for a simple reason. I knew that General Tolimir worked in the same military district as I did. There were meetings, there were briefings, and I heard the name during those events. And finally, I personally met the general in 1992 when I arrived in that area and when I took the position that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Did you have any encounters with General Tolimir during the war after that first personal contact, and how often did you see him during the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: During the war, from May 1992, I met General Zdravko Tolimir on several occasions. Our encounters were during meetings, briefings, inspection visits, debriefings. I can say that on several occasions, or at least a dozen times, General Zdravko Tolimir inspected my unit and the other units that were deployed in my area of responsibility. Those meetings and encounters were always with a view to getting an insight into the situation in the units in the territory of responsibility and the issues that they were facing. Depending on weather conditions, on time limitations, my conversations with General Tolimir were always friendly, amicable. Whatever we were requested to do was with a view to improving the situation, our attitude towards the troops, our attitude towards the officers, and there were all the other issues that were of some relevance as a result of General Tolimir's inspection visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Let us now focus on the events that took place in 1995, the events that are of some interest for this Trial Chamber. My question is this: In July 1995, did you have an occasion to see any members of the Main Staff in the area of your responsibility or elsewhere? Thank you. And I mean any of the members of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of July 1995 when the Croatian military offensive began against the territory of Republika Srpska, there was an increased presence of officers from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. In my area of responsibility and beyond, I had an opportunity to meet first of all with General Milan Gvero and his associates from the superior command, as well as with General Tolimir and the late General Djordje Djukic. In my area of responsibility, while carrying out combat operation along the Donji Vakuf-Travnik axis, the command was visited by General Gvero, who inquired about the situation; and in late July, the command post at the Jajce garrison, General Tolimir paid us a visit and he was particularly interested to hear about the situation on the front line and in the units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Can you tell us, can you remember, When did you meet Gvero and when did you meet the other individuals that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I saw General Gvero at the Jajce garrison and thereupon he inspected my unit. And that was on the 27th of July. I remember this date precisely because that was the day of the uprising of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So rather jokingly we asked the general whether he had come to congratulate us on this holy day and whether he brought any presents with him. Secondly, in those days, after the Croatian offensive on the 28th of July, my town of Glamoc fell, and these are the dates that help me recall that General Gvero was there at the time. I remember that two or three days later another group of officers from the Main Staff arrived and I met with them at the Jajce garrison. Among them was General Tolimir as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, Do you know where this group from the Main Staff was located when they came to visit your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: The group of officers from the Main Staff who had arrived in the zone was billeted in a facility within the Kula barracks, after that at the Petar Mrkonjic barracks, and they remained there all through 1995 until Mrkonjic Grad fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For the record, can you tell us where the Kula Kasarna is situated?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: The Kula Kasarna, or, rather, the Petar Mrkonjic barracks, is 6 kilometres from Mrkonjic Grad on the Mrkonjic Grad-Kljuc road, between the villages of Rudici and Jovandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber something about the activities of your brigade and the axes that your brigade covered in defending Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: My brigade, the 1st Sipovo Light Brigade, as it was named during the war, carried out defence operations along two axes. The first one was the Donji Vakuf-Travnik axis at the Komar pass. They carried out defence operations along the front line which was about 30 kilometres long. In total, we had approximately four battalions engaged in these activities. The second axis that the brigade carried out defence was the Sipovo-Kupres axis, where we had a combat group which equalled, in strength, three battalions. This combat group was called Janj combat group. I have to tell you that following the fall of Glamoc and Grahovo and after the enemy had reached the vicinity of Mrkonjic Grad, elements from my brigade were engaged in the operation of closing the Mrkonjic Grad-Kljuc road, and other on the Mrkonjic Grad-Jajce road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please, is the village of Bjelajac [Realtime transcript read in error "Bilajac"] in your area, and can you tell us on which road it is situated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: The village of Bjelajce is seven kilometres from Mrkonjic Grad on the Mrkonjic Grad-Banja Luka road, and it was approximately three kilometres within the territory of the forces defending Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, From your superiors who were holding these axes, did you have any information that in the territory of the village Bjelajce there were refugees from Sipovo and Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, I personally had an opportunity to see that the civilians who left Glamoc on the 27th and the 28th were provided accommodation in the general area of Mrkonjic Grad municipality, including at the school in Bjelajce. I know about that because all of my folks also fled Glamoc and I was keen to find out whether they were alive and well and if I could provide some assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as for the other people who hailed from Glamoc, did they come to Bilajac in order to see the refugees from their native town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Of course. Everyone feels a strong pain when it comes to their native towns or villages, especially if information was scarce as to their whereabouts. Everybody wanted to offer a helping hand, not only to us who came from Glamoc, but to everybody else. I clearly remember that we discussed the issues of how we could help all these refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just for the sake of the record: Mr. Culic, could you please repeat the name of that village you are talking about and spell it, please, letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can do that. B-j-e-l-a-j-c-e.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We had some different spelling on the record. Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You just said that you had meetings and that you discussed how to help the people. With whom did you meet in that village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Among others there were lots of people from the corps command and people from the Main Staff. The first one with whom I had a meeting was the late General Djukic, and after that I met with you and we had a discussion. I was particularly interested in the condition of the combatants in the area because all of my next of kin was in the unit that was defending Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, Can you remember approximately when you and I met in Bjelajce?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I think that was three or four days after my meeting with General Gvero, and I think that that was on or about the 30th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have Exhibit P2458, page 2. Thank you. It's page 3 in English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, on page 2 we see the title: "The Bosansko Grahovo and Glamoc area." And then look at paragraph 3 and I'm going to quote it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would appreciate if we could see first the first page so that we know about the document itself. Then we form a better understanding. We want to see both first pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we first see page number 1 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, perhaps you can briefly introduce this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is a document produced by the intelligence administration of the Croatian Army entitled: "Intelligence Report," of 30th of July, 1995. It was printed in Zagreb on the 31st July, 1995, in Zagreb. And it describes the state and activities of the SVK, VRS, and VJ. They produce such intelligence reports on a daily-basis, and in this report they say the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we can go to the pages 2, respectively, and 3. Thank you for this introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, as you can see in this chapter entitled "The Bosansko Grahovo and Glamoc area," the third paragraph reads: "During the day General Tolimir and General Djukic from the VRS Main Staff have been sent to the Grahovo Glamoc front line in order to consolidate the situation and undertake measures to consolidate the forces. To this purpose, a special team, ZM," means "joint command," "will be set up at Drvar --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please move to the next page in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "... which will be led by General Milovanovic following the directive of M. Karadzic," although it should read "R. Karadzic." My question is this: Since this document that comes from the Croatian Army was drafted on the 31st, as I said earlier, can you tell me if this period, according to what you know, was the period when General Tolimir was in the area of your brigade or, more precisely, along the axis where you carried out your activities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I think that the time-frame is correct and I think that was exactly the period when you were in the area of Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us the exact place where we met, and you said that we did meet; tell us where it was.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: We met for the first time on that day at Bjelajce and then on the same evening in Jajce at the division command post. I can also tell you that at the time my command post was at the Jajce garrison and so was the division command post. The two were only a hundred metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Tell the Trial Chamber some more about your knowledge about General Tolimir's movements from the time when you met until the end of the war, as far as you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to meet General Ratko [as interpreted] Tolimir at least ten or 15 times in those areas. And those were both official and unofficial meetings, or encounters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, Mr. Culic. I just want to clarify one matter. You said: "We met for the first time on that day in Bjelajce ..." Which day was it? Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said about three days after the 27th, so it would have been on the 30th or 31st. I think it was the 30th, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue with your answer to Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since at that time the situation on the front line was extremely bad and difficult because the offensive of the Croatian Army and the BH Army had begun along all axes, it was necessary to take all organisational measures and other measures for the system of command and control and combat readiness that had been disrupted by the actions of the NATO aeroplanes. And command was very difficult, so we had to restore that system back to normal. Under these conditions, all the measures that the units and commands took to stop the offensive and repel the attack, we had debriefings each evening and even earlier than the evening when it was necessary. There were also meetings for the purpose of analysis. Those meetings were held at the division command. Very often somebody from the Main Staff organs would be present as well. Apart from that, on the ground, that is, on the battle-field, it was necessary to assess the situation in the units and take adequate measures. Since the defence system, the old defence system, had been disrupted, adequate measures were taken by the Main Staff officers or, rather, the forward command post of the Main Staff headed by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Culic, you said that some measures were being taken. Here's my question: Did any officer from the Main Staff command any subordinate unit in the zone of responsibility of your corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I must be very clear about this. The exclusive right to command and take decisions was with us, commanders. After the meetings and analyses at command level, we received clear and precise orders from the superior command, that is, the division command. So those officers didn't command our units. They were only there to assess the situation from their level and set tasks to the units through the testimony of command and control, and it's clear how that went: by way of orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information if the Main Staff, or, more precisely, General Tolimir, stayed in Western Bosnia for a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that I had the opportunity to meet him rather often. Secondly, we met a couple of times at the front line while defending Mrkonjic Grad or actually immediately before the fall of that town, and I'm talking about a period of at least a month or two. And we must have met some ten or 15 times at least. But even when we didn't meet for a couple of days, I did have such information, because we, brigade commanders, exchanged information about things. So I did have information whether anybody was going to negotiations, or not, and so on. I was able to learn that from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. Not everything was recorded when I started speaking. Did you know where the forward command post of the Main Staff in that part of your zone was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the forward command post was where I was, at Kula, and I knew, roughly, where they were and how things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to make a correction for the record. Page 14, line 9 -- no, sorry, 8, the word "testimony" should be replaced by "system." Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us anything about the situation on the ground from August until the end of November in the zone where your unit was active in 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: From July till October 1995, the situation at the front was extremely difficult for two reasons: One, the Croatian Army and the BH army had launched their offensive ; and two, NATO forces and the rapid-reaction forces had also launched their actions. They started bombing our command posts and communications hubs of the VRS. In such a situation which was bad both for the VRS and my unit, it was necessary to keep the territory, preserve the unit, and certainly the population, too. In this time-period, following the loss of some territories from which the Serbian population was expelled, Glamoc, Grahovo - after that, Drvar, Sipovo, Kupres, Donji Vakuf, Kljuc, and finally Mrkonjic Grad - a less favourable balance of forces came about. From that time-period, from July until October or until the signing of the Dayton Accord, my unit, like other units that were engaged in the defence of those areas, were in a very unfavourable tactical position. At times, command was very difficult because our radio relay hubs had been destroyed. NATO planes had bombed that facility at Rajakovo Brdo near Mrkonjic Grad. Besides, the units were always in an unfavourable position because there was an imminent threat of air-strikes. In such a situation, everybody made an all-out effort, both the rank and file and the officers, to stop the enemy and engage in active defence. During that time-period, we were able, owing to the great efforts of the fighters of the VRS, to stop the advance. And we slowed down the attack of the HV and the BH army after some 20 or 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the losses that the population incurred during the NATO air-strikes and the actions of the rapid-reaction forces as well as those of the HV and the BH army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally have such information, among other things because I was in that area even after the war and I was able to see that there were victims, because while that -- when that radio relay hub was attacked, four soldiers got killed in 1995. After that, upon the signing of the Dayton Accord and the return of the population to that area, we found over 180 killed civilians in Mrkonjic Grad municipality alone. But there were more in the areas of Sipovo, Glamoc, Drvar, and other places that had been occupied by the HV forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it logical, then, for the Main Staff to have forward command posts in an area where the aggression of third countries and NATO forces against the RS was being slowed down and was that one of the reasons why these officers were in Western Bosnia where your brigade and your corps were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Clearly the Main Staff assessed the situation, and it was the gravity of the situation in the theater of the Western Krajina, where there was an aggression of the HV forces, was the reason why they went where things were worst. And I am sure that there was a command post there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your previous answer you mentioned a relay station that was bombed by NATO planes. You mentioned its name. But do say next to which facility it was and who was staying at that facility. Which soldiers are belonging to which unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I mentioned a short while ago that one of the facilities targeted by NATO planes was the radio relay hub of Rajak, which was on Rajakovo Brdo, which is some 500 metres away from the Petar Mrkonjic barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a forward command post of the Main Staff in that barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was also a forward command post of the Main Staff, which was probably one of the potential targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were involved in these events, and you have also explained who else was involved, did you during that period and later understand who was attacked there and who was an ally in that attack and in the combat?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, clearly everybody of us was clear about the fact that the Croatian Army had entered and occupied a part of the territory. Also that the BH army had an ally in the NATO forces that bombed us, not only the Croatian Army as an ally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. During the war, since you joined the VRS, you were a brigade commander all the time; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. I was brigade commander for 11 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were brigade commander, can you tell us whether there were rules and regulations in force in the brigade that the officers, both active-duty and reserve officers, had to abide by?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Upon my joining of the VRS, the Republika Srpska and its army had adopted the rules and regulations that were in force in the Yugoslav People's Army. Everything that had been set out in the rules and regulations governing the activities of the Yugoslav People's Army. I know that for sure because I was a member of the JNA, too, and I know that all the rules and regulations governing our combat activities were those that were in force in the JNA as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, during the war, did we also adopt rules from any of the other republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: No, we did not receive rules from any of the other republics. However, as the Army of Republika Srpska, whenever a rule or a regulation had to be amended, for example, if we are talking about the dress code, and so on and so forth, we would receive such an amendment, an amendment of the dress code. And those amendments became an integral part of the rule that was already in force, and all our members were duty-bound to comply with the amendments of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the amendments in question apply only to your dress code or perhaps even to combat activities and combat operations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I believe that only the -- the only thing that happened was that the Army of Republika Srpska adapted to the situation at hand in keeping with the strategy and plans of the use of units that were drafted based on the rules for the use of brigades, corps, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stopped you again because you started too early. Please repeat your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, for the record, could you please tell us, What combat rules are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the combat rules of the former JNA. We're talking about combat rules for the infantry battalions, infantry brigades, and other instructions about the work of the command staffs and institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Thank you. Do you know who in your brigade commanded the military police, for example? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my brigade I was in command of the military police. I was in command of all our -- my units, including the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, please tell us, Was the security organ in a position to command the military police in your brigade or in any other brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in our organisational structure we had security organs who were our immediately subordinated officers. Their professional element and the work that they did - and that was provided for by the rules of the work of organs and services - envisaged that in the process of decision-making, those professional organs proposed the ways how certain tasks would be carried out. However, the exclusive right of command and use was in the hand of the commander. As you know, whenever a task was distributed, the situation would be assessed and the decision-making process followed. During that process, every organ had the right to suggest how the task should be carried out. Once the proposals were looked at, the commander was the one who made the final decision, irrespective of the fact whether the proposal was proposed by any of the organs, because the commander was responsible for his decision and he had the exclusive right to command and control. And I can say for a fact that in my brigade, or any other brigade, nobody else had the right to command, and that included a security organ or any other organ. The only person who could command was the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Who was in command of your security organ in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I was the one who commanded my security organ. And that was the exclusive right of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your brigade also have an intelligence organ in addition to the security organ?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: In addition to the security organ who was subordinated to me as the commander there was also an intelligence organ, but he was the assistant Chief of Staff for intelligence, which means that he sent his proposals and he reported to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Who was the Chief of Staff? Was that somebody outside of the brigade or in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: He was the assistant of my own Chief of Staff for intelligence. And if he was his assistant, it was only normal that he reported to him about his tasks. So not to any other Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Your security organ and your intelligence organ, could they receive orders from the security organ of your superior command, for example? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the rules were very clear. The system of command and control was very clear. All the orders followed that system of command. When it came to certain information, intelligence, certain analyses, certain issues pertaining to professional and specialist training, obviously the organ of the superior command would send that mail to us, and then that organ informed us about, for example, the activities of the enemy, and everything else that did not interfere with the system of command and control. However, primarily, as I have just told, you security organs did not receive orders from the superior security organs. They were their superiors only in terms of professional education.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Culic, can you tell us, for the record, Was Tolimir in a position to command the security organ and the intelligence organ in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, knowing General Tolimir personally, I have to be very clear: He never requested to do that. He never did that because he was very familiar with the system of control and command and he would not have wanted to humiliate either me or any other commander by giving orders to his security or intelligence organs. I know personally that General Tolimir, when he visited my unit on several occasions before 1995, he even spent several nights with my unit. He never wanted to impose himself as an officer from the Main Staff who had the last say. He always showed understanding for us. He always wanted to listen to us, to hear us out, and to propose the best measures. And all the measures that were undertaken in order to implement certain tasks were implemented pursuant to the orders and commands of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Thank you for having come to testify in these proceedings. I thank you for everything. I thank you. I wish you God-speed in your future life and work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions for this witness. We have brought our cross-examination to an end -- I apologise, it was an examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Culic, now the Prosecutor, Mr. Elderkin, has the opportunity to put questions to you. But before he gets the floor, Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Culic, regarding your last answer, you told General Tolimir that he never wanted to humiliate anybody and that he was always ready to listen to everyone. But knowing full well that he was the person in charge of security and on the information -- security and information, rather, how was he able to give you his instructions and his orders? How -- how would he give you those instructions, in which manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, General Tolimir never arrived in my unit on his own. He arrived with other officers who were my immediate superiors from my command, from the 30th [phoen] Division. He did not arrive in my units to issue orders. His primary purpose was to look at the situation on the ground. He wanted to obtain information from us and he wanted to receive information from us. He did not come to issue orders. I don't know if you understood my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you very much. Yes, yes, you were quite clear. Thank you very much. But, yes, precisely after assessing the situation, after getting all the information from you, he would take certain measures, he would take certain decisions, so how was he able to apply these measures that he had taken which -- in which way? Through which channels was he doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, as I have already told you, we held regular meetings and briefings in our commands. At those meetings and briefings we received tasks from our commanders, from our superiors, with all the precise details of the measures that had to be undertaken. And that was imparted not only to the general, but everybody else who came to visit. So he did not issue orders to me directly. Those orders were handed down from the most superior command down the line of command to the lowest units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question to you. I understand that you had a very friendly conversation with Mr. Tolimir during these meetings, but sometimes it's possible that a superior officer is not satisfied with the information he receives, or not satisfied with the situation he finds. In which way he could influence the situation to improve it? In which way could he react to the information received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, as subordinates and junior officers, we always valued the advice of our superiors. Obviously, on the ground, if certain things were done, we sought advice as to how to do them. However, nobody ever came to us and ordered us about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Elderkin, please commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to Your Honours and to everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, good morning to you. My name is Rupert Elderkin, and I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I want first, please, to cover your knowledge of General Tolimir's whereabouts during the period of the fighting in the Krajina in the summer of 1995. You've told us that the first time that you met General Tolimir in July of 1995 was in Bjelajce and that was on the 30th or the 31st of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said that you met General Tolimir on about ten to 15 occasions during the course of the defence of the Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you also said that General Tolimir remained in the Krajina area throughout that period until at least the fall of Mrkonjic Grad. Does that correctly reflect what you've testified to this morning, Mr. Culic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Are you aware that General Tolimir travelled away from the Krajina on a number of occasions during August, September, and October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I know that from time to time he would go to attend meetings, negotiations, and things like that. I don't know how long he stayed there, but I know that he returned to the area. At the end of the day, when it comes to his departures and negotiations with the enemy side or NATO, we could read about that in newspapers. It was covered by the media extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: But there is no specific reason why you personally would have known about General Tolimir's whereabouts day by day except on the occasions when you met him personally in the Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I just want to clarify the time-frame when you say that General Tolimir remained, generally, in the Krajina area. You said it was until around the fall of Mrkonjic Grad. Can you please tell us on what date Mrkonjic Grad fell, as best you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Mrkonjic fell sometime in October 1995, in the first half of October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you recall, when was the last time that you met General Tolimir, either a date, or, if not, do you recall the circumstances of your last meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember that I saw him between Rogolji village and Mrkonjic Grad on the road from Mrkonjic Grad to Kljuc. I met with General Tolimir and General Gvero late in the evening. I was there because I headed a unit in the direction of Mrkonjic Grad. I remember that it was the beginning of October, sometime around the 6th, 7th, or perhaps the 10th of October, in any case it was in the first half of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So to be clear: The ten to 15 times that you met General Tolimir were between around the 30th or 31st of July and sometime up to the beginning or middle of October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mid-October.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as a means to save time in covering questions about General Tolimir's whereabouts during this period, I have prepared and have loaded into e-court a summary of the dates and the corresponding evidence the Prosecution has concerning General Tolimir's presence at locations outside the Krajina region. This isn't a piece of evidence. It's something that I've prepared myself but as a means to present more simply to the witness and to Your Honours what evidence we have about General Tolimir's whereabouts in August through October. I'd ask, with your leave, that I could show this to the witness and the Court. It's something that we gave to the Defence at the beginning of this week, and, of course, I'd only go ahead with your and their agreement, but I believe it would be an efficient means to proceed, rather than going through the binder of documents I have one by one. It bears 65 ter number, provisionally, 7619, and I also have hard copies if that would assist people more easily, both in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, could you explain a bit further the purpose of putting this to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has told us that he generally understood General Tolimir to be in the Krajina area, obviously away from Eastern Bosnia, away from the VRS Main Staff, throughout the period in question, and in the 65 ter summary for this witness it was indicated that this evidence should be relevant to certain paragraphs of our indictment - I think 23 and 23.1 - which concern other events that were happening at that same time. The evidence that I would like to take the witness through is to ask the witness whether he would agree that on many occasions General Tolimir did, in fact, travel to Eastern Bosnia, attend meetings with various significant individuals, including, on many occasions, with General Mladic and others, and that took him away from the Krajina and back to areas of Eastern Bosnia that are geographically relevant, obviously, to our indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understood the testimony of this witness that he only was able to tell us about his meetings with General Tolimir between the 30th of July and, at the latest, 10th of October, 1995. Is this a period which is relevant to our indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the period in question is that which is when the reburial operation was under way in Eastern Bosnia, in the Zvornik and Bratunac municipalities. It's also the period when certain of the men who were captured after the fall of Zepa were incarcerated. And then during August and September those men were killed. If I understand General Tolimir's position in leading this evidence, he seems to be seeking to establish his distance from those events. If not, then I wouldn't see any relevance in having called this witness to testify about his whereabouts in that time-period. If the evidence in chief about his whereabouts is relevant, then I would submit that on cross-examination it's both necessary and proper for the Prosecution to be able to go into those questions of whereabouts in that period. But if Your Honours consider that General Tolimir's whereabouts is not in issue when considering the events in the indictment of August, September, October, in terms of the reburials and the foreseeable killings, then it's not a subject that, obviously, I would need to cover on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not what I said, but I just wanted to clarify your position on that. Mr. Tolimir, what is your position in respect to the request of Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have not used this witness to prove exactly where General Tolimir was on each and every day. We just discussed those periods when he saw us, when he heard that we were in his area of responsibility, in the area of his responsibility of his corps or brigade. We don't want -- if Mr. Elderkin has proof that we participated in the events, that we were in the area at the time, we invite Mr. Elderkin to present them for the benefit of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber is satisfied with this explanation of Mr. Elderkin. If it relates to the time-period 30th of July up to 6 -- no, 10th of October, 1995. That is the period the witness testified about and was examined by Mr. Tolimir. We can do that after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'd ask, simply because of the way I prepared the document itself - it contains entries for the last three dates in October which are the -- well, two dates, sorry, 14th and 27th, which appear on the sheet, because I've prepared it through to the end of October - if I were to restrict myself up to the 10th of October, would it be acceptable, still, to use the same document? Otherwise, during the break I can try to retype this and load a new copy into e-court. But if we can just ignore the end of the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are only referring to evidence which is admitted during this trial. That -- therefore, I don't have a problem with that, if you restrict your examination to the period we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And to be absolutely clear, Your Honours: There are some items on here which bear 65 ter numbers which have not yet been admitted but which I have on my list to use with this witness. But I would certainly restrict myself to the indicated period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have our first break now, and we will resume five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin. You may proceed as discussed before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it's agreeable, I would propose handing out hard copies of this reference list because that way I can leave it on people's desks while we work alongside other documents in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, with the assistance of the Court Usher. Would it be helpful to put one copy on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is possible. I've handed up four copies for the Bench, also for the Legal Officer. Unfortunately, I don't have a fifth for the ELMO. So if I could ask to keep one of the four or simply that everyone has one. There are three in B/C/S for the witness, Mr. Tolimir, and Mr. Gajic. So I think that there's no need to put it on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, in a moment I'm going to ask you about various times when General Tolimir was outside the Krajina. But since you told us the period in which he remained in your area of the Krajina, and that was until sometime in mid-October --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like, please, to see Exhibit D264.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- and just confirm with you your understanding until the time until which General Tolimir remained in your area and what was he doing when he was there. Now, on the first page of this document, Mr. Culic, you can see that this is an order issued by the Main Staff of the VRS, and it's an order to the corps level, and its subject is: "Blocking the Enemy Offensive on the Western Republika Srpska Front."

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could go, please, down to the bottom of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think we can see the start of various instructions under point number 5. And this item starts by saying: "a) "Main Staff of the VRS to direct the entire operation, engaging the following commanding officers ..." Sir, do you see that text at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you saw this document before when you testified in the Popovic case. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I may have seen it. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You agree that at point 5(a) there is reference to engaging certain commanding officers, at the bottom of the page, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: That's the only thing that I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Then can we go to the next page, please, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You see at the bottom that it's an order from General Mladic; do you see that, sir, at the type-signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at the top of the page, please. And what you can see here, by each dash, is a reference to different members, different generals of the VRS Main Staff, and each is assigned specific tasks. So, for example, the first is an assignment for the Chief of Staff, and that's General Milovanovic. Do you see that right at the top of the page, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, if we go down to the sixth, I think, dash, you should be able to see a reference to General Tolimir. And you see that just before the gap in the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And there it reads, for General Tolimir's assignment --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- "Assistant commander for intelligence and security, Major General Zdravko Tolimir co-ordinates action by the 30th PD, defending the axis Mrkonjic Grad - village of Trijebovo - village of Stricici and is responsible for the defence of the axis." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you agree that at the beginning of this point in the order, point 5, General Mladic was referring to the following officers as commanding officers, because this operation, this defence, was to be supervised and overseen by the Main Staff. That's what it says in the document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And General Tolimir's assignment here is to lead and to be responsible for defence on the axis mentioned, beginning with Mrkonjic Grad. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Gentlemen, General Tolimir did not lead the operation. He was there merely as a representative of the command in order to co-ordinate the work to the extent that it was necessary on the battle-field to achieve co-ordinated actions. In command were the commander of the division and the commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: General Mladic is specifically assigning General Tolimir and making him responsible for the defence of the mentioned axis; is that right? He's responsible for it according to this document.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it clearly says here in the order that he is to co-ordinate the work. There is no responsibility of his. Responsibility lies with the unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned earlier that Main Staff officers, including General Gvero, General Tolimir, visited the Krajina from the end of July onwards. You said that they inspected your unit. Almost all of the Main Staff generals came over to the Krajina when the Croatian offensive started, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if all of them, but most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the reason for bringing the Main Staff generals to the Krajina was to strengthen and steer the defence that was being put up by the VRS forces in that area. They were there because it was a serious situation and these were serious generals who had to be responsible for their defence of the Republika Srpska territory. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier, within the system of command and control it is the commander who is responsible for the implementation of decisions, whereas the organs of the superior command only assist. You can also see in this order that he is to co-ordinate the actions of the forces on that axis where the defence operation for Mrkonjic and access is to Banja Luka, and there were several units and several corps engaged in that operation, which means that co-ordination was necessary in terms of the timing and the method of carrying out tasks. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you were referring to the word "co-ordinates," but the end of the sentence reads as follow: "... and is responsible for the defence of the axis." What is your understanding of the word "responsible" in that context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand it to be that he is responsible for co-ordination and organisation of the forces that are engaged in the defence. Because, along these axes leading to Mrkonjic Grad and Banja Luka, there were units from other organic formations and that necessitated a co-ordinated action in temporal and spatial terms and that is where their responsibility lie. In the course of carrying out each specific task, whether it be defence or reconnaissance or whatever, those who are responsible for these tasks are unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please see 65 ter number 397. First of all just the front page so we can identify that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, while this is going to come up in front of you in e-court, let me tell you that this is the VRS Main Staff analysis of the combat readiness of the army in 1992. So from earlier in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I'd like, please, to go to page 160, 1-6-0, in English, and page 139 in the B/C/S. And if we could go -- scroll down the page in the B/C/S so we can see the part that begins in -- "In Posavina..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the paragraph there now just below the centre of the page, starting: "In Posavina and Western Bosnia ..."?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Let me read through it. It's only a short paragraph. "In Posavina and Western Bosnia, we have put the emphasis on the grouping of forces, air and artillery support, and in Podrinje, in a specific way, the increased expenditure of ammunition and materiel and equipment, as well as the use of the reserves of the Main Staff of the Army of RS. The presence of the commander of the Main Staff, or of a representative of the Main Staff, in the units carrying out the mission of the liberation of Podrinje in a specific way of giving weight to and steering combat operations towards a single goal." So that's just the sort of thing that the generals of the Main Staff, including General Tolimir, were doing when they were sent to the Krajina in the summer of 1995, isn't it? They were giving strength to and making sure those units were focused on the goal, as ordered by General Mladic. Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, their presence definitely contributed to a better performance of the tasks. But this order also definitely shows that the Main Staff has its own focus, just like every other unit has the focus of its action. Therefore, the order says that the commander is going to be either at the command post, forward command post, or an observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, the Prosecution agrees that commanders issue orders in the VRS, but would you agree that General Tolimir and other specialist assistant commanders and other security and intelligence officers were experts in implementing the orders of the army's commanders?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All the assistants were experts in their respective fields of expertise, but they were not those who implemented the orders on the ground, because the system of control in our system was quite clear: The orders were carried out by the commands or institutions; that is to say, commanders of division, corps, battalions, platoons, et cetera. And that is on -- the basis on which our chain of command was constructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to, please, go to one of the documents that's mentioned on the list everyone has in front of them. It's the first reference. And this is for August, the date of the 6th of August, and this is a time when General Tolimir attended the 52nd Session of the Republika Srpska National Assembly in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 3455, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, do you know if General Tolimir was in Pale on the 6th of August of 1995 attending this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that he did attend certain Assembly sessions. But if I look at this date, I can only conclude that according to this document he attended this session as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could please go to page 35 of the English and page 31 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you can see here General Tolimir is one of the speakers at the Assembly session. Do you see his name at the top of the page, sir, followed by the transcript of what he was saying that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the English --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I can see his full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: For everyone's reference: In the English it's right at the time at the bottom of the page. So we need to scroll down, please, to the foot of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, sir, we've already discussed the role of the generals of the Main Staff when they were assigned to the front lines. In particular, you've told us about General Tolimir in the Krajina in July. Where did General Tolimir come from? What front was he at before the Krajina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I really can't tell you where he had come from. All we knew was that he had come from the superior command. As for his movements, I really cannot tell you anything about it because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You know about the operations to take over first the Srebrenica enclave and then the Zepa enclave in Eastern Bosnia which took place in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that this happened in July. But I don't know who was there, who was moving about, or what they were doing. I really had no connection with any of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: General Tolimir was assigned in Eastern Bosnia and he was in Zepa until just before he came to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we go to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, you are at the moment a bit beyond the area Mr. Tolimir raised in his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you will allow me to continue with the next couple of questions, this returns to the subject of the responsibilities of General Tolimir in a command or an operational role, and it's discussed in this Assembly session as well as in additional documents. I can show you the page, Mr. President, and hopefully you will see where this is going. It's at page 32 in the B/C/S and page 37 in the English. And it's starting in the indented paragraph right in the middle of the B/C/S page and also the middle of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It starts - and this is General Tolimir responding to another speaker: "A statement that Zepa was a reason for the fall of Glamoc and Grahovo, because two generals were assigned to Zepa, has been used as a trump card here. By solving the problem of Zepa, dear gentlemen, we got two brigades from Drina Corps in the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps. By solving the problem of Srebrenica, we also got adequate reserves. And we did it in the period of time for which we estimated that the international community would not react, which was immediately after the events that took place in the Western Slavonia." Do you see that part, sir, and does that reflect that General Tolimir was assigned to Zepa in a role involving the oversight of the take-over of that enclave which, according to General Tolimir himself, succeeded in relieving the pressure on the VRS and thereby assisted in providing troops for the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. I see in front of me a lot of things mentioned by the Prosecutor, but I don't know with whom Mr. Tolimir spoke with, what kind of report he is talking about, whether there were two or three generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Well, sir, you can read for yourself, in the text in front of you, General Tolimir's statement about two generals being assigned to Zepa. I believe it's uncontested in this trial that General Tolimir was present as a general of the VRS Main Staff during the VRS operation against Zepa. And you can see that that operation, according to General Tolimir, led to the successful completion in Zepa, and that liberated units of the Drina Corps to go to the Krajina. Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What you are asking me about? Because if I read it, I can't see, from what I see, to whom General Tolimir spoke, so your question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, this is the record of the RS National Assembly. General Tolimir is speaking at that Assembly. He's responding to another speaker, but he's addressing the Assembly. And this is a record of the minutes of that. So General Tolimir here is speaking to a wide audience. In any event, sir, I'll show you something else, if I may, which is a short video-clip. And this is of General Mladic. And General Mladic here is discussing what role or part of the role that General Tolimir played during the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this is from Exhibit P1029.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, I don't quite understand this line of questions you are putting to the witness. We discussed earlier in which way your questions during cross-examination should relate to the examination-in-chief. If -- you should tell us in which way you could establish the whereabouts of Mr. Tolimir during that period we talked about by showing this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage my examination is focussing on one of the other subjects of examination-in-chief, which is what kind of role General Tolimir did and could play when he was assigned to one of the fronts of the VRS's combat actions. General Tolimir came, as we know, straight from Zepa across to the Krajina, and in the Assembly session minutes he described that assignment, how two generals had been assigned in Zepa, clearly responsible for the Zepa operation. The speech, as shown on this video, General Tol-- General Mladic - excuse me - describes one of the activities that General Tolimir undertook during the Zepa operation. So it's following that part of the examination-in-chief in terms of the responsibility. Because it's reflected in this 6th of August Assembly session, I found it more convenient to go straight to the video which talks about that subject. It doesn't, obviously, deal with his whereabouts in August. I can stick to the whereabouts line of questioning first, but it did seem to me to be natural. If you would prefer that I save that until we've been through other documents concerning the whereabouts first, I can also do it that way, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was just wondering what purpose you are heading at. But if you are now talking about command structure and command responsibilities of assistant commanders or members of the Main Staff, you may do that because that was one part of the examination-in-chief. But that was not clear from the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I apologise for lack of clarity. That's where the video is going. I will return also to the whereabouts during the period August through the beginning was October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Correct me if I'm wrong: My understanding of the evidence-in-chief related to the period 30th of August to somewhere in the middle of October. And as I have understood the evidence - correct me again if I'm wrong - Zepa operations happened before 30th of July. So do you think you are within your area of cross-examination focussing on Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Your Honour. My cross-examination in relation to Zepa is to respond to the part of the examination-in-chief where General Tolimir was asking the witness about his understanding of what role he, General Tolimir, as an assistant commander could perform in relation to military operations. Not just the Krajina operation, but, obviously, the representation is that General Tolimir in the Krajina, if he was unable to give orders, direct military activities, that would also apply for any consideration of the role that General Tolimir played during the earlier operation. So at this point I'm moving away from the whereabouts, but it is focussing on that important part of the examination-in-chief. And it's for that reason I'm talking about Zepa; not because, obviously, the witness was far away from Zepa and not present, I understand, during that operation, but because of the question of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And we could see the clip, please, which is at 2 hours, 12 minutes, and 55 seconds through to 2 hours, 13 minutes, and 42 seconds. And that reflects, for point of reference, the transcripts of the same video, which in English is at page 11 and B/C/S at page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd ask you, please, to listen carefully to the part of General Mladic's speech when he speaks about General Tolimir and a person called Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can we play it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May we stop for a moment. We can't hear. I think even the witness can't hear it very properly. It's very -- it's not loud enough. But perhaps you can help us with the translation: Is there -- are there subtitles or do we have a transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: There is, indeed, a transcript. I don't see any subtitles, so I doubt very much that there is a subtitled version available in the system. The transcript, I think, is associated with the same exhibit number. And, as I say, the page numbers for this section are page 11 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S. It may be -- since it's only a very short clip of under a minute, perhaps we could just play through and -- for what it's worth and then have up on the screen the two transcript sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please. I agree. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, we are going to put on the screen now a written transcript in case General Mladic's words there weren't clear enough for you to hear well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And as I say, I think it's page 8 in B/C/S and page 11 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, if you see in the lower half of the page, you can see a section beginning with the name of General Tolimir. The video we've seen started a little before that and played through to a little after that. The part concerning General Tolimir reads: "From Boksanica, General Tolimir and Kusic fired on Ribioc." Do you see that section, sir, of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Here General Mladic was speaking about General Tolimir playing what was clearly an active role in the military attack on Zepa by firing on that village. Do you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Gentlemen, as far as I know, General Mladic mentioned three officers. General Tolimir, who probably represented the Main Staff, was among them. I know that Kusic was a brigade commander, which means that it wasn't him who acted. It was his unit that acted. So that was the brigade under the command of Colonel Kusic. And he was there, obviously, to represent the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I am finished with using the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the video already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The video is, Your Honours. The Assembly session minutes are not. I would propose to tender only a short range of pages for the section that I referred to, as well as, perhaps, the first page, to give an indication of the date. So that would be pages 1 and then 35 through 37 in English, and page 1 and 31 through 33 in the B/C/S. And that's for 65 ter number 3455.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you intend to upload these pages as a separate document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I understand that that's the easiest way to proceed, so yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After having uploaded this separate document, it will be marked -- it will be received. But this document, 65 ter 3455, will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And it will be assigned Exhibit P2878. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, I'd like you again to look at the list of places where the Prosecution say General Tolimir was present outside the Krajina during August through October of 1995. I only want to go to a couple more examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The next one would be 65 ter 2494, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this is again an Assembly session. It's the 53rd Assembly Session, and it's in Pale. It takes place on the 28th of August of 1995. And if we could first see the cover page. So you see the date and the title of this. It's the minutes of that session.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can we first go, please, to page 14 in English, page 18 in B/C/S. We can go to the bottom half of the page in English, please, and it will be the -- yep, the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's fine right now in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So you see the paragraph which talks about European peace negotiations. It starts with "I will tell you about some details here later ..." and then it describes a couple of meetings of peace negotiations; one in Geneva on the 16th of August and a second time in another European city on the 26th of August. And then it reads --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- "The first time the talks were conducted by President Krajisnik, Mr. Zametica, our side, asked that we don't send more negotiators. And the second time, on the 26th of August, President Karadzic, Mr. Lukic, General Tolimir, President Krajisnik, and myself." Sir, do you agree that this indicates General Tolimir was away from the Krajina at European negotiations on the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that day, for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Then can we please go to page 22 of the English, page 28 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you see here that General Tolimir spoke at the 53rd Assembly Session on the 28th of August? He was also away from the Krajina on that day and he was in Pale that time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask to tender a couple of these pages. There is, actually, an exhibit, P2435, which contains the section we're seeing on the screen now. It doesn't contain the previous page, page 14 in English, page 18 in B/C/S, of which refer to General Tolimir's attendance on the 26th of August at the other negotiations. So I only want to put in, again, the cover page, and then page 14 in English, page 18 in B/C/S, which we can upload separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is appreciated. And it will be received. And until that point in time it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be assigned Exhibit P2879. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, without going into every other document, do you agree, as a general proposition, that there were numerous occasions when General Tolimir was away from the Krajina during August, September, and October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I know that he spent some time in Krajina. I also know that he had tasks that took him all over the place. But he also returned.
