I don't have any doubts about the documents that you're showing me. I don't doubt their authenticity. When there was an Assembly meeting, I'm sure that he was present. So I'm not contesting anything here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like, please, to see Exhibit P104, which is a collection of maps. And go to page 4, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this will be uploaded: Mr. Elderkin, you have used 65 ter 397, "The Analysis of Combat Readiness." Are you tendering parts of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Excuse me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask to tender the whole document. If, however, Your Honours will only allow a part to be admitted, it would be the section that I read from. But I believe that the whole document is a relevant analysis. It's not contested as to its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- authenticity. I believe the English is 149 pages and the B/C/S, I think, slightly shorter. It's 109, off the top of my head, but I can check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't object to the admission of anything that this Court deems to be evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I remember properly, this analysis was also used when Mr. Butler was examined in this courtroom, or perhaps the OTP relied on it. Maybe we should check whether one part of that analysis is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that Mr. Butler does, indeed, cite to this report in his own reports. We're not sure if -- off the top of our heads, if he actually testified about it, but it's certainly material that he uses in his reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told by the Court Officer that a part of this analysis is already in evidence, tendered through Witness Butler, as P2491, but not the whole document. Now you are tendering the whole document, and the translation is already available; therefore, it will be received as a separate document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 397, the complete document, shall be assigned Exhibit P2880. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And if I could now have P104, at e-court page 4, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have one map on the screen. Is that not the correct one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That is the correct one. If we could zoom in as much as possible onto Bosnia to keep it within the edges. I think a few centimetres we can go past. Yes. I think that's perfect, thank you. I'd also ask if the witness would be able to mark on this map just so we can be clear where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- he was engaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, the Usher is going to show you how to use this electronic pen to draw on the screen. First of all, do you confirm you recognise this map which shows the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? And roughly the different shading areas represent the -- the borders of the entities. I understand that things were moving around in the summer of 1995, but the part in the west, that's the Krajina area where you were based. And Republika Srpska forms this wider shape, narrows off up around Bijeljina, and then runs north-south along the eastern side of Bosnia. Could you mark on there, please, sir, a circle -- a reasonably large circle where you were engaged, where your brigade was located in the summer of 1995. As a point of reference: Just below the S of Bosnia is the town of Sipovo, of the centre of Sipovo municipality.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please mark it. That area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us which -- the first line that we see on the map that runs through the federation territory, what does that represent, if anything? Is that the front line at the time? Or ... all I can see at the moment is a longer line and then a short vertical line. What does the longer line represent?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: The longer line is the axis of my brigade from Donji Vakuf to Travnik. It encompasses the zone on the right, excluding Bugojno; and on the left, Mount Vlasic. The second part of the brigade which was Janj combat group, or Combat Group 1, encompassed the road across Kupres and all along the border from Glamoc to Vitorog. The third smaller part, when the offence was launched, that part of the brigade covered the axis in the direction of Kljuc, i.e., Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this is the area where General Tolimir was president -- present - excuse me - when he was in the Krajina in the summer of 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This area is even wider, because the territory of Krajina extended all the way to Drvar, so this did not cover only the area where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And in the summer of 1995, for anyone - General Tolimir or anyone else - who wanted to travel from the Krajina through Republika Srpska territory to get back to the VRS Main Staff at Crna Rijeka or to get to Pale, they would have to travel all the way through the Republika Srpska territory that we can see on the screen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a road. They moved in vehicles or in helicopters. It all depended on the task at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we just concentrate on the road, that would mean travelling from the area where you've put your markings northwards towards Banja Luka, then across and through the corridor to Bijeljina, down past Zvornik, Vlasenica, to Han Pijesak or even further to Pale. That would be roughly the road route, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes. The road led to Banja Luka. Banja Luka was the cross-roads either towards Prijedor or Prnjavor or towards the corridor. In any case, that was the road that was used for travels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. I don't need for you to make any more markings and I don't need to use this map any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So I'd ask if this could be saved, unless Your Honours wish to add anything else to what's marked now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering this marked map?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I may, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 4 of Exhibit P104, marked by the witness in Court, shall be assigned Exhibit P2881.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you referred to NATO bombing of various communications facilities. You didn't give us a date for that bombing. I'd ask you if you agree that NATO's bombing campaign was starting on the 30th of August of 1995? That's the date when many of the VRS communications facilities was bombed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: It was a long time-period. I don't know exactly when that started, but I know that communications centres and radio hubs were bombarded by NATO. I know that we received air alert signals every day. My area of responsibility was often overflown by NATO. One NATO aircraft was even grounded in the general region of Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like the return to the subject that you mentioned earlier about the ability of security officers to give orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I'll first ask, please, to show Exhibit P2176. Your Honours, this doesn't appear on my cross-examination list. It's an area that only came up during the examination-in-chief. The exhibit is already admitted, so hopefully it doesn't cause any problem for the Defence that it's being used now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you can see here a document headed from the VRS Main Staff security and intelligence sector, and specifically from the security administration. You see that at the top of the page. If it would help, we can zoom in.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page do you see that this document was written, signed, and sent by Ljubisa Beara? It's under the round stamp on the left at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you happen to know who Colonel Beara was? Did you ever serve with him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I never served with him, but I know who he was. He was the chief of security in the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, sir, this telegram from Colonel Beara -- actually, he signs here as "Naval Captain Beara." This is addressed to the security section of the East Bosnia Corps, as well as security section of the Drina Corps, and to the chief of intelligence and security of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. You see that just below the heading, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: To the chief of the security organ, I would say, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if you just take the time - it's a short communication - to read through. At the end of the first paragraph, there's reference to Atlantida must be transported in secret to the Mlin military prison in Bijeljina in the night of 10th to 11th of June, 1995, or at some other appropriate time. Captain Carkic will arrange this with brigade commander Major Rajko Kusic and personally carry out the task by announcing his arrival to Colonel Todorovic, chief of the OB IBK and explaining our demands in person. Sir, do you agree that here Beara is issuing orders to his subordinates in the security service to carry out a very specific task; namely, the transport of this Atlantida to the Mlin prison? He's instructing and ordering his subordinates here, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, he's issuing instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And those instructions were to be followed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see from the document, he was giving instructions and guidelines to the organ as to how they should carry out this task. And he also conveyed to them that this professional task that they have to carry out, that it will be performed in agreement with the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, we've also heard testimony in this case about General Tolimir giving orders or instructions to subordinate security officers, specifically that he sent a telegram to the East Bosnia Corps. And this is around the 12th of July of 1995. That preparations should be made at the Batkovic collection centre for the arrival of 1.000 to 1.200 prisoners. That's again an example of security officers being able to issue orders or instructions within their service, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask Mr. Elderkin to show the witness the telegram that Tolimir sent on the 12th to East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would agree with Mr. Tolimir. It would be helpful for the witness, and for a better understanding of the Chamber, to see the document you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'm referring to the testimony of another witness in the case, and that's of Witness Todorovic, Your Honours. And that's at reference 12933 to 12934 of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have that on the screen. And you should point out the lines you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If it will help to locate it, it's the 18th of April, 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you can see, starting at line 23 of page 12933, an answer given by the witness, which starts: "Yes. I cannot really be specific about the date. I couldn't do it in Belgrade, I cannot do it now, as to whether that was on the same day in the evening or the following day or two days later, but in any case, it was after the fall of Srebrenica, I think, and I am 90 per cent sure that a telegram came from the Main Staff that the East Bosnia Corps command should be engaged and should prepare accommodation at the Batkovic collection centre for another 1.000 to 1.200 -- 1.100 or 1.200. So 1.000 to 1.200, as far as I can remember. Thus to prepare accommodation for new detainees who are going to be coming over the coming days." And so the testimony is that this order came from the security and intelligence sector from General Tolimir. Sir, as indicated by this witness's testimony that I've read to you now, the instructions about making preparations for a receipt of prisoners were instructions which were issued with the intention that they be followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Elderkin please show the witness where it says that he received an order from Mr. Tolimir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I've read all that I need to read from the transcript, and hopefully my question is clear. I've read out the section referring to this telegram. I'm now asking the witness whether those instructions -- the word "order," if General Tolimir wishes I don't use it, I can say "instructions" -- it's what this witness doesn't know any more about what happened in the East Bosnian Corps in terms of receipt of that telegram order or instruction, but my question relates to his knowledge about what would happen, what was meant to happen, on receipt of such a communication from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand your position, Mr. Elderkin. But in your question you presented already an interpretation and your understanding of this part of the transcript. I don't see the name of Mr. Tolimir in that part of the transcript. Not even his sector in the Main Staff. I only can read that a telegram came from the Main Staff, that the East Bosnian Corps command should do that and that. It's better not to put too much of your own interpretation into a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Well, I can restrict my question and re-ask it as follows, if it's acceptable:

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: An instruction issued by the Main Staff - and I refer to the instruction insofar as you can understand it from what I read to you of the other witness's testimony - such an instruction from the Main Staff was issued with the intention that it would be followed, the instructions would be carried out. Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Of course the Main Staff issued orders that should be followed. They would not issue any orders that are -- are not to be obeyed and carried through. They can issue orders orally or in writing, or they can convey them through communications means, or they can be carried by a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that it would be important to read lines 8, 9, and 10 on page 12934 which would clarify whether it was a written order or a telephone conversation. So the Trial Chamber can then discern from this what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. That is just a proposal. And all this is on the record in this case. Mr. Elderkin, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And just in relation to that discussion we've just finished, that we agree that the full testimony of that witness needs to be read to understand exactly what instructions were issued, but I'm not going to ask any more questions on that particular subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, do you know the word "balija," which refers to Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with it because I still live in the place where there are Muslims and Croats. This word dates back to ancient times and it is used as a derogatory term among ordinary folks when they talk about Muslims. They call them "balijas."

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, in communications that you sent as a brigade commander during the war, did you use the word "balija" when you were referring to Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I personally don't use that word. However, whether it was mentioned in any of the documents, I wouldn't dare to tell you anything with 100 per cent certainty. Anyway, I would like to say that this word does not exist in my vocabulary because my whole life and throughout my schooling - and I worked in an institution that trained Muslims, Croats, Albanians, all other ethnicities - and for that reason, I cannot tell you for certain, but I can tell you that I, myself, don't use that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the Prosecution would agree with that, sir. We've looked at many of your combat reports and other documents that you wrote during the war and which we have in our evidence collections, and we can't see anywhere that you used the word. Does that sound fair?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, it does sound. But I told you that it is 99 per cent true. Because, as you know, sometimes you don't always draft documents yourself. People do it for you. You only sign it. Sometimes you don't have time to read it before signing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: An officer using the word "balija" in a communication would convey an unprofessional message, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Possibly. But all kinds of terms were used during the war. The other side did not refrain from using various words. War is a specific phenomenon and I really wouldn't like anyone to experience that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Would you agree that using the word "balija" would have the effect of dehumanizing the Bosnian Muslims much more so than somebody using more neutral terms such as the "Bosnian Muslim side" or "the enemy"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if you look at it today, and if you take everything into account, that would be so. But you know that during the war there was a lot of belittling and demeaning and insults, et cetera. Nowadays it wouldn't be politically correct, but at the time it was being used and it was something normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can we see Exhibit P2274, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It's a short document, sir, and you can see that it was sent by General Tolimir of the VRS Main Staff on the 4th of June, 1995. You can see that it's sent to some important people here, including the president of Republika Srpska. And you can see -- if we go down a little bit in the English just to see clearer, there's a paragraph -- the first paragraph, which reads: "The GS VRS commander and his staff maintain the positions presented in this telegram regarding your proposals for resolving matters of additional exchange of prisoners of war with the Ustasha and balija side." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this kind of language coming from General Tolimir is unprofessional and insulting and derogatory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, as I told you: At the time, words were being used that could possibly not be permissible today. Just as we used to call them balijas, they used to call us Chetniks. So let me be clear on that. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can Mr. Elderkin show the -- whether this document was signed by General Tolimir or by somebody who authored it, because there's no signature here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you may deal with that in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I can confirm, though, Your Honours, there's nothing else except what is on the screen at the moment. So what you see, as I understand it, is what we have. And I've finished my cross-examination, Your Honours. There is one matter I'm asked to mention to you, which is that for 65 ters 7621 and 7622, P numbers 2878 and 2879 respectively, that are MFI'd, the excerpts have now been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case these two documents will be received into evidence. Mr. Tolimir, now it's your time to examine the witness during your re-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we see document D64 that the Prosecutor has used. Thank you. D264. I apologise. That's the document. I asked for the document that was used by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Culic, this document was shown to you by the Prosecutor. And in the bottom paragraph, which at the moment you cannot see, which is actually at the very bottom of the page, so can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Item 5, tasks of unit, it says: [As read] "The Main Staff of the VRS to direct the entire operation engaging the following commanding officers." Now, my question is: Who is directing the operation, the Main Staff or the officers that they appointed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: Did the Main Staff direct all the operations --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you. You were overlapping again. We want to have your full answer on the record. Please wait, always, and pause between question and answer. Now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire combat operation in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina was directed by the Main Staffs of the VRS through its relevant institutions, organs, commands, and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. If any of the officers engaged along the axis mentioned herein, if he were to have some suggestion or some remarks, did he have to pass it on to the commander of the Main Staff, or could he order this to your unit or any other unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait. Please wait. We want to have everything on the record. Now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the command system, all orders arrived through the command in charge. Likewise, every order that arrived from the Main Staff would first go to the corps command, then the corps commander would pass on the order to brigade commanders. That is the essence of the system of command and control that was applicable both in the VRS and in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. My next question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's time for our second break, and you may continue after the break. We must have our second break now, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, while the forward command post of the Main Staff at Kula existed, did you receive an order signed by any of the officers of the Main Staff who were stationed there at that forward command post of the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: General, sir, and gentlemen, I can say with full certainty that I never received a written order from the Main Staff save for information which was sent along the information line, and I'm talking about the alert signals. The only orders I received, I received from my division commander or my corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just been informed that "alert signs" were not recorded properly. Can you repeat: What alert signs did you receive?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Those were air-raid alert signals and nuclear, chemical, and biological alert signals. Those two signals had priority when it came to informing, and they were conveyed immediately, independently of who had issued them. As for all the other orders, they were conveyed, as I've already told you, through orders and commands that could be issued in a written form, they could have been issued verbally, or they could have been conveyed via the courier service or via appropriate officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether an officer of your command that you would have sent to your 3rd Battalion, for example, could he change your order issued by yourself to that battalion - a combat order - and could he have ordered that battalion to act contrary to your original order? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I stopped you again because you started too early. We want to have everything on the record. Now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The officers of my command would go to subordinated units daily. They would go there pursuant to various tasks, and they received those tasks from the commander, meaning me. Those orders dealt with various issues. An officer who goes to a subordinated unit cannot change an order, which means that my officer could not change my order. If the order dealt with a certain issue that may have been pointed [as interpreted] by an organ of the command, the officer would convey that to me. When I accepted the change to that order for the implementation of a task, then I could change the order, I could accept the proposal, or I could alternatively reject the proposal. In conclusion, I would say that things are clear. The only person who could change an order or task was me. Nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P2274.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a telegram dealing with exchanges. It was shown to you by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, please, you see a telegram on the scene. The telegram was type-signed by Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. My question is this: When it comes to this telegram, should it have been signed by somebody before it was sent for coding? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I know that before the war and in the course of the war, and even after the war, all the mail that was sent in a coded form had to be initialed or signed. A telegram of this nature containing an order sent by whoever could not be coded without being signed first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. And now could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we please see the next page in the English, to have the signature block and the stamp on the screen. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, the author of the telegram, was he duty-bound to sign his name and did he have to indicate the name of the person who typed it if he didn't do it himself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please pause after having received the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, everybody who processed a document that had been drafted and copied in several copies, be it a combat document or any other type of document, as part of any office correspondence, has to contain in the left-hand-side corner the initial of the person who processed such a document as well as the initials of the person who typed the document and who dispatched it, who sent it off. This is how things are done in nearly 99 per cent of the cases. At the bottom of the document you will find the initials of the person who processed the document; i.e., the person who actually drafted the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Please, we can see a document which doesn't contain either a signature or initials that you talked about. Obviously this was due to the fact that the document is not original. It's not the main departing document. This is a telegram. Does a signature have to show on the telegram?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: No. This is a document without a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, tell us, instead of the person who was supposed to sign the document, could the document be initialed by his deputy by preceding their name with the word "za" or "on behalf of" if he is authorised to do so? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Within the system of the organisation and establishment of units, there is a provision which stipulates who has the right to put their signature on what documents. Moreover, it is also stipulated who can act on behalf of somebody else and sign certain documents on behalf of somebody else in the absence of the person who would normally be authorised to sign them. All documents must be signed either by the authorised officer or a person standing in for that officer in his absence. And in that case, the document signed in that manner is as valid as a document signed by the officer who is the order issuer. The brigade commander is deputised by the commander of the staff in his -- absence from the unit, and he can sign all the orders drafted by the commander on his behalf. Or any other authorised organ in the command or in the institution of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. If you had the original document with the signature or the initials, and if that document was not a telegram, would you be able to establish who signed it and who drafted it, who the author of the document is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: If there is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: If there is the original of the document bearing a signature, obviously you can establish who signed it. But if such a document doesn't exist, there are no guarantees to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic, for having come to testify in these proceedings. Thank you for your testimony. I would like to apologise to you for making you wait for two days due to the situation as it was. I would like to thank you. I wish you a happy return home. May God-speed be with you, and at the same time may these proceedings end in accordance God's wishes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Thank you, general.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. I have a final question in relation to this document we have on the screen. Could the two stamps be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Culic, we agree that there was no signature near to the signature block. Now you can see a stamp on the left side in original, and it was translated into English on the right side of the screen. What can you make out of this stamp? Was this stamp put on this document on the sending side of the telegram or on the receiver side?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it says here that it was received, so the receiver was the one who put his signature on the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: His stamp. The interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The receiver, did he -- from where did he receive this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: The receiver could receive such a document for only one place. When you initiate the coding or decoding process, in this case to -- you either type it on an instrument or you inscribed it by hand. These are the only two ways in which he could receive this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Look at the third line. There we see the word "processed." How do you understand this word?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: The person who processed the telegram is the same person who received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Processed where?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: Well, it was processed there, at the encryption office where the telegram was received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You see at least two signatures on the right side of the stamp. Can you read the signatures? Can you read the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, the name is Stanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a person with this name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO CULIC
utterances.text: I really don't know who that might be. There are many of them with that name, but I personally don't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation. Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes now your examination here in this trial. The Chamber, like Mr. Tolimir, we would like to express our apologies that you had to wait several days until the commencement of your testimony. Thank you for your patience and thank you that you were able to provide us with your knowledge and your expertise in this field. You are now free to return to your normal activities. Thank you very much, again. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish you a pleasant day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, Mr. Tolimir, are there any matters to deal with at the moment? Taking into account that we will have a housekeeping session next week. I don't see any. Then I would like to take the opportunity to say some words because this was the last witness in this trial, witness number 130. We were together quite a long time, and I would like to express my gratitude to the staff. First and foremost to the Victims and Witnesses Section. At another occasion I forgot them when I mentioned several units, and therefore they are the first we have to thank, because without them we would not be able to have any witnesses in our courtroom. I would like to thank the security staff for their contribution to making this trial possible. To the whole courtroom staff, that means the courtroom officer who was and is for a long time already with us; the various court ushers; the court reporter; the interpreters, who do a lot of work and without their work we would not be able to communicate in the courtroom - a specific thanks to them - but also to the translators. Without their work we were not able to read all the documents. I would like to thank the technical staff, the IT people who helped us with the problems we encountered sometimes here in the courtroom. And I would like to thank the staff of the Chamber, two of them are present in the courtroom, and the staff of the parties - both sides. And I would like to thank the parties themselves for the good co-operation, for the fruitful co-operation during this trial. I wish you all the best. We adjourn for this week, and we will resume next week on Tuesday, 9.00, in this courtroom, for the housekeeping session. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
